title: Maha Shivaratri (the night vigil)
hook: the night is split into four watches, and something is poured over the lingam in each one

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi's goodbye: the clay given back to the water, and come early next year. What did you let go of? Today, a night you don't sleep through. Day one hundred forty-eight.

An all-nighter has a shape. Students cramming for an exam know it, new parents know it, nurses on the night shift know it. The buzz around eleven. The slump at two. A strange clear stretch around four. And the gray light that feels like a reward. On Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, whole temples keep that shape on purpose, with no deadline at all. You heard the hunter's story on day eighty-three, the man who stayed awake in a tree by accident. Today, how the night is kept on purpose, watch by watch.
screen: `AN ALL-NIGHTER HAS A SHAPE.` → `A WHOLE TEMPLE, ON PURPOSE.` → `WATCH BY WATCH.`

segments.voice: Maha means great. Shiva, the auspicious one. Ratri, night. It falls on the fourteenth night of the waning moon in late winter, the darkest night before the new moon. The day begins with a fast. Many people eat nothing, or only fruit and milk. Then, at sunset, the vigil starts, and it has a shape. The night is divided into four watches, called praharas, each about three hours long. In many temples and homes there's a worship in each watch: the lingam is bathed, and in some traditions each watch gets its own offering. Water, or milk, or yogurt, or ghee, or honey. It's called abhisheka, and it's the heart of the night: pouring, slowly, while chanting. Then bilva leaves, three to a stem, laid on top. Between the watches, people sing, read stories of Shiva, and chant the mantra from our mantra week, its five syllables na-mah-shi-vaa-ya, usually with Om before them: Om Namah Shivaya. Some count it on beads through the whole night. The word for staying awake like this is jagarana, keeping awake. And here's what the four watches do. A whole night is too big to hold. Four watches of three hours, each with one thing to pour, are just about possible. The night stops being a wall and becomes four doors, each opened in turn. When dawn comes, people bathe, make a last offering, and break the fast. Some who keep the vigil say the last watch, just before sunrise, is the clearest part of the night.
screen: `MAHA, SHIVA, RATRI.` · `A FAST, THEN SUNSET.` · `FOUR WATCHES, FOUR POURINGS.` · `JAGARANA: KEEPING AWAKE.` · then, large: `A NIGHT BECOMES FOUR DOORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: four small watches. Settle, and breathe. Split this sit into four, the way the night is split. First watch: just arrive. Notice where you are. Second watch: picture water poured, slowly, over a smooth stone, and let your breath pour out the same way. Third watch: the slump. When your mind drifts, and it will, just come back. That's the whole job of the third watch. Fourth watch: the gray light. Sit very still, as if dawn were just starting. If you pray, you can say Om Namah Shivaya once in each watch. The bell holds the time.
Maha Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, kept awake in four watches, with water poured over the lingam until dawn.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri, the night vigil. Today, break one big thing into four watches, and open them one at a time. Day one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, keep a vigil through the four watches of the night, bathe the Shiva lingam with water, milk, yogurt, ghee or honey, offer bilva leaves, and chant Om Namah Shivaya until dawn.

Cut the sweeping 'Nobody says it's easy. Everyone says it's worth it.' and the superlative 'the quietest and clearest hour of their year'. 'Five-syllable mantra ... Om Namah Shivaya' corrected: the panchakshara is na-mah-shi-vaa-ya, with Om usually added before it.
